title: Pay depends more on the occupation than the city, but some regions pay a clear premium
question: What do people in common newcomer occupations earn, and how much does it differ between places?
dek: Job Bank wage estimates for ten occupations: low, median and high hourly wages of employed workers, by economic region.

findings.headline: Median hourly pay across 10 common newcomer occupations ranges from $17.31 (retail salespersons) to $48.08 (software developers)
findings.detail: Canada-wide medians for employed workers run from $17.31/hour for retail salespersons to $48.08/hour for software developers, a ratio of 2.8x. Within an occupation the low-to-high range is wide: software developers run $30.00-$76.92. These describe people already working in the occupation in Canada, not starting pay for new arrivals.
findings.calc: Job Bank Wages 2025 edition, geography Canada (ER00), median wage for NOC 21232, 31301, 73300, 42202, 11100, 72200, 63200, 64100, 44101, 72106 (all hourly, Annual_Wage_Flag=0); ratio = max median / min median.

findings.headline: Registered nurses' median hourly wage is $48.01 in Calgary but $39.38 in Québec City (provinces, same occupation)
findings.detail: Among the places' economic regions in the ten provinces, the highest published median for registered nurses and registered psychiatric nurses is $48.01 (Calgary economic region) and the lowest $39.38 (Québec City), a gap of $8.63/hour. Territorial medians are higher still (Whitehorse $48.50, Yellowknife $58.00, Iqaluit $57.99). Remote places also tend to have higher living costs; wages here are nominal and not adjusted for prices.

stat.label: Gap between highest and lowest provincial place median

findings.calc: For each place take the median wage of NOC 31301 in its primary economic region (geo.economicRegions[0]); shared ERs counted once; gap = max - min over the 10 provinces' places, territories reported separately.

findings.headline: Welders' median wage in Calgary and Edmonton ($37.72, $39.90) is about 39% above Toronto and Montréal ($28.00, $28.00)
findings.detail: The pattern is similar for transport truck drivers: $30.00 (Calgary) and $28.85 (Edmonton) versus $25.10 (Toronto) and $23.68 (Montréal), about 21% higher. For child-care, retail and food-service occupations regional differences are much smaller. Always compare against local rents before treating a wage gap as a gain.

stat.label: Welders: Calgary/Edmonton mean median vs Toronto/Montréal mean median

findings.calc: Median wage NOC 72106 (welders) and 73300 (truck drivers) in primary ERs of the four places (4830, 4860, 3530, 2440); percent = mean(Calgary, Edmonton) / mean(Toronto, Montréal) - 1.

interpretation: Use the occupation first: the spread between occupations is far larger than the spread between most cities for the same occupation. Regional differences matter most for trades, truck driving and health care, where Alberta, British Columbia and the territories sit at the top.

The low wage in several occupations is identical across occupations within a region (for example $17.60 for cooks, retail and food-service workers in Toronto and Ottawa), which looks like a minimum-wage floor, so low-end figures partly reflect legal floors rather than market pay. Median and high values say more about experienced workers.
Credential recognition, licensing and Canadian experience can put new arrivals below these medians at first, especially in regulated occupations such as nursing.
methodology: Source: Employment and Social Development Canada, Job Bank Wages (open data, 2025 edition, revision date 2025-11-19). Wage estimates are for employed workers by NOC 2021 unit group and economic region; they are not advertised wages.

Estimates come from the Labour Force Survey (2023-2024), Employment Insurance survey data, Small Area Estimation (2024) and, for a few occupations, the 2021 Census; the source of each cell is in the open file.
Each place is represented by its primary economic region (the first economic region listed for the place). Values are nominal hourly dollars; all ten occupations are published hourly.
Occupations were chosen for newcomer relevance (high-demand, large and regulated and trades occupations) and for data availability; occupations with an annual-rate flag were avoided.
limitations: Economic regions are not the same as cities: Vancouver and Abbotsford-Mission share one region (Lower Mainland--Southwest), Québec City's primary region is Capitale-Nationale, and Montréal's is the Montréal region only (not Laval or the suburbs).

Small Area Estimation and LFS-based estimates carry sampling error; cells without enough data are not published and are left empty here (not replaced by provincial values). Missing places per occupation: Software developers: Iqaluit, Thunder Bay, Whitehorse, Yellowknife; Electricians: Whitehorse; Welders: Iqaluit
Reference period is 2023-2024 (mostly); wages have moved since. Wages are not adjusted for local prices and exclude benefits.
